title: Acme AI escalation: streaming timeouts / connection resets (SUP-1842)
summary: Acme reported intermittent streaming disconnects/timeouts in us-east causing truncated generations and retry storms in their proxy layer. Redwood confirmed elevated stream reset errors starting ~15:40 UTC and that the issue presents as mid-stream connection close with no final chunk. We agreed on a customer-side mitigation: (1) implement idempotent retry with jittered backoff and cap, (2) increase client/read timeout for streaming and ensure keepalive settings are sane, (3) temporarily disable HTTP/2 for the streaming route / force HTTP/1.1 where possible, and (4) log/capture request_id for every failed stream for faster correlation. Redwood will keep incident comms via email every 60 minutes while impact persists (and within 30 minutes for material changes), and will move to 2x/day updates once stabilized. Next steps: Redwood SRE to post an internal incident bridge update + share a short customer-safe root cause statement; Support to attach request IDs + timeline to SUP-1842; Docs to publish the workaround article and link it in the ticket; Engineering to prioritize improved error messaging and routing metrics for Support validation.
topics: Symptoms: mid-stream disconnects, truncated output, client timeouts
Scope: us-east primarily; hosted inference streaming endpoints
Immediate mitigations: retries/backoff, timeout tuning, HTTP/2 disable, keepalive
Diagnostics: request IDs, SDK version, proxy behavior, correlated dashboards
Comms plan: cadence, what goes to status page vs direct email
Next steps: SUP-1842 updates, KB workaround publication, engineering follow-ups
action_items: Redwood (Sean Gallagher): Confirm current error-rate and whether mitigation has reduced stream resets; provide customer-safe incident summary by EOD 2026-02-03
Redwood (Priya Shah): Update SUP-1842 with agreed workaround steps + request ID examples from Acme by 2026-02-03
Acme (Miguel Santos): Ship temporary config to force HTTP/1.1 for streaming (or disable HTTP/2) on the edge/proxy and report result within 2 hours
Acme (Lena Hart): Provide 10-20 request IDs from failures + approximate timestamps and SDK versions by 2026-02-03
Redwood (Rachel Kim): Send customer email recap + comms cadence (hourly updates) immediately after call
Redwood (Owen Phillips): Open/ensure linkage to known-issues article draft for streaming timeouts and cross-link from SUP-1842 by 2026-02-04
next_steps: Acme to deploy HTTP/2-off mitigation and confirm whether disconnect rate drops
Redwood to continue hourly email updates while incident ongoing; faster updates for material changes
Redwood to publish KB workaround and provide link for Acme runbook
Follow-up call scheduled for 2026-02-04 to review stability and any residual impacts
questions: Is the reset happening at the proxy (idle timeout) or server-side close from Redwood gateway/runtime?
Do failures correlate with longer generations / higher max_tokens or specific models?
Can we narrow impact to streaming only vs non-streaming completions?
Should we post a status page update vs keep comms direct to Acme only?
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-03
Start time: 17:05 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Title: Acme AI escalation: streaming timeouts / connection resets (SUP-1842)
Attendees (Redwood): Rachel Kim, Owen Phillips, Sean Gallagher, Priya Shah
Attendees (Acme): Lena Hart, Miguel Santos, Priya Desai, Nate Wong

Summary (auto)
- Customer reports streaming disconnects/timeouts leading to truncated responses.
- Redwood confirms elevated resets in us-east and shares immediate mitigation suggestions.
- Agreement on workaround steps, required diagnostics, and update cadence.


[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright. Thanks everyone for joining on short notice. This is the Acme escalation on streaming timeouts, tracked in SUP-1842. I want to use this time to (a) confirm symptoms and scope, (b) align on mitigations you can apply right now, and (c) align on comms cadence so you’re not chasing us.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Yep. Appreciate it.

[00:20] Miguel Santos: Thanks, Rachel.

[00:22] Rachel Kim: Owen is our incidents SME from Support, Sean is SRE on-call partner, and Priya is helping us capture the steps into the ticket and the doc.

[00:31] Owen Phillips: Hey everyone.

[00:32] Sean Gallagher: Hi.

[00:34] Lena Hart: Hi, Lena here. So the issue: streaming responses are cutting off mid-generation. It’s not like we get an error chunk; the connection just closes. Our client treats it as a timeout or reset. Then we retry and we end up with duplicate work, plus some user-visible failures.

[00:55] Rachel Kim: Got it. When did it start for you?

[00:58] Miguel Santos: We noticed around… 15:40 UTC, maybe a bit earlier. But it spiked at like 16:10.

[01:06] Lena Hart: We’re primarily us-east. We have some eu-west but this seems us-east heavy.

[01:13] Sean Gallagher: That matches what we’re seeing. There is an elevated rate of stream resets on the us-east gateway path. Not a total outage, but enough to hurt. We’re actively mitigating.

[01:26] Nate Wong: What does “mitigating” mean in this context? Like you’re shifting traffic, or rolling something back?

[01:33] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, it’s a combination. We adjusted some routing and connection handling parameters. I don’t want to over-speculate on root cause yet. But we do have a strong signal it’s localized to streaming and a subset of connections.

[01:48] Owen Phillips: For Support purposes: the common signature is “stream ended unexpectedly” and the client sees a reset. It can show up as truncated output or missing final tokens.

[02:00] Rachel Kim: Lena, can you share what SDKs you’re using and if you’re behind a proxy or something that might be enforcing timeouts?

[02:08] Lena Hart: We’re using your TypeScript SDK in one service, but most traffic is via our internal gateway that calls your REST streaming endpoint directly. It sits behind Envoy. Envoy has HTTP/2 enabled by default to upstreams.

[02:23] Miguel Santos: We also have an idle timeout on downstream, but this is happening within like 10–30 seconds sometimes, not like a 60-second idle thing.

[02:33] Sean Gallagher: That’s helpful. One thing we’ve seen with a few customers is HTTP/2 + intermediaries can amplify stream reset behaviors when upstream has transient issues. A pragmatic workaround is to force HTTP/1.1 for the streaming route. Either disable H2 to Redwood for that cluster or set it per-route.

[02:53] Lena Hart: Okay. We can try that. We can carve out a cluster just for your streaming endpoint.

[03:00] Priya Shah: I’m going to capture that as “temporary mitigation: disable HTTP/2 for streaming path; force HTTP/1.1.”

[03:08] Rachel Kim: Great. Second thing: what are your client timeouts for streaming?

[03:12] Miguel Santos: We have a 30-second per-request timeout in the gateway. It was fine historically.

[03:18] Owen Phillips: For streaming, we recommend not using a strict wall-clock timeout that’s too low because token cadence can vary, and retries can cause storms. Better is a read timeout per chunk plus an overall max.

[03:31] Lena Hart: We have a read timeout and a total timeout. But I think the total might be 30s in one service.

[03:38] Sean Gallagher: I’d suggest increasing overall timeout for streaming to something like 120s, depending on your max_tokens. And the more important piece is how you retry.

[03:49] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk retry strategy. Are you retrying immediately on disconnect?

[03:54] Miguel Santos: Pretty much. We do immediate retry twice. No jitter. And we’re seeing that cause load.

[04:01] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, so: jittered exponential backoff, cap it, and ideally enforce idempotency so a retry won’t duplicate work if the first one actually completed but you lost the tail.

[04:14] Lena Hart: For streaming, idempotency is tricky. We can attach a request key and de-dupe at our layer, but your API doesn’t accept an idempotency key right now, right?

[04:23] Owen Phillips: Not universally. Some endpoints support a client_request_id field depending on SDK version, but not as a hard idempotency guarantee. However, de-duping on your side with a stable key per user action is still useful.

[04:37] Priya Desai: Our bigger concern is user experience. A retry often returns a different completion. That breaks workflows.

[04:45] Rachel Kim: Understood. For the immediate window, we’re trying to reduce outright failures. For determinism, if you can set temperature to 0 and keep seed stable where supported, that can reduce variance, but not perfect.

[05:01] Sean Gallagher: Also if the disconnect occurs, you can attempt a “resume” pattern by reissuing with the already received prefix as context, but that’s application-specific.

[05:11] Lena Hart: Yeah, we can’t do that easily. But we can do temperature=0 for some flows.

[05:17] Rachel Kim: Let’s ground on what we can agree on now: 1) force HTTP/1.1 for streaming, 2) increase streaming timeouts, 3) jittered backoff retries with cap, 4) capture request IDs for each failure.

[05:33] Priya Shah: What do you have today for request IDs? Are you logging the x-request-id header or the response header from Redwood?

[05:40] Miguel Santos: We’re not consistently capturing it. We can.

[05:44] Owen Phillips: That’s huge for us. In SUP-1842, if you can paste 10–20 request IDs and timestamps, we can correlate exactly which gateway instances were involved.

[05:55] Nate Wong: In the streaming response, where do we get the request ID? It’s in headers only, right?

[06:02] Owen Phillips: Typically yes, headers. Some SDK helpers also expose it. But if you’re using Envoy, you can log upstream response headers.

[06:11] Sean Gallagher: And please include the region you’re hitting, but you said us-east. If you’re using a global endpoint, tell us what DNS resolves to.

[06:20] Lena Hart: We use the us-east endpoint directly. No global.

[06:24] Rachel Kim: Good. Sean, can you share current status? Like are things improving?

[06:30] Sean Gallagher: In the last 20 minutes, resets are down but still above baseline. We’re watching error rate and the “streaming health” panel. We’re not calling it resolved.

[06:42] Priya Desai: Are we in incident mode? Should we be looking at a status page post?

[06:47] Rachel Kim: Good question. We have internal incident tracking, but status page updates depend on breadth and customer impact. Right now it’s not a full region outage, and it’s streaming-specific. But Acme is materially impacted, so we’ll do direct comms regardless.

[07:03] Owen Phillips: If it expands or we see clear multi-customer impact beyond tolerance, we’ll push for a status page event. But we don’t want to post something that’s not accurate.

[07:15] Miguel Santos: We’d prefer transparency. Even a “degraded streaming” note is helpful.

[07:22] Sean Gallagher: Understood. Let us evaluate after the next mitigation step. I can’t promise status page right this second, but we will keep you updated.

[07:32] Rachel Kim: Let’s align on comms cadence. Given enterprise expectations, we propose: email updates every 60 minutes while impact persists, and within 30 minutes for any material change (e.g., identified cause, mitigation applied, or worsening). Once stabilized, we can go to twice daily until fully resolved + postmortem.

[07:55] Priya Desai: Hourly is fine. But we need something our execs can forward.

[08:00] Rachel Kim: We’ll keep it customer-safe and crisp. We’ll avoid speculation.

[08:05] Lena Hart: Can we also get a Slack connect channel?

[08:08] Rachel Kim: For this incident, we can keep it to email to avoid splitting context, but if you prefer Slack connect, we can discuss. Owen, what’s standard?

[08:17] Owen Phillips: Generally for escalations we do email + the SUP ticket as system of record. Slack connect can be helpful, but we need to ensure we’re not doing real-time backchannel that bypasses incident comms. For now, let’s stick to hourly emails and update SUP-1842.

[08:34] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[08:36] Priya Shah: Also we’re publishing a short workaround doc that you can share internally. It’ll basically say what we’re saying: disable HTTP/2, timeouts, retry policy, capture request IDs, when to escalate.

[08:48] Lena Hart: Great. We need something copy/paste.

[08:52] Rachel Kim: Let’s go a bit deeper on your Envoy config. Miguel, do you have max stream duration or upstream idle timeouts?

[09:00] Miguel Santos: Upstream idle is 15 seconds I think? Wait, that’s downstream. Upstream might be 60. I need to check. But we’re seeing disconnects sometimes at 8 seconds.

[09:14] Sean Gallagher: 8 seconds suggests not purely your idle. It could be upstream closing. But disabling H2 can still help because H2 resets propagate differently.

[09:24] Lena Hart: We can push the H1.1 change quickly. Probably within an hour.

[09:30] Rachel Kim: Perfect. We’ll treat that as the first experiment. Please measure before/after: failure rate, average stream duration, and any change in latency.

[09:41] Priya Desai: Our user-facing symptom is truncated answers. So we can measure “incomplete completion” and “retry count.”

[09:50] Owen Phillips: That’s great. Also, in SUP-1842, note whether the truncations happen at similar token counts or random.

[09:58] Lena Hart: It’s random. Sometimes like 30 tokens, sometimes 400.

[10:05] Sean Gallagher: Random token count is consistent with a transport reset, not a model-side stop.

[10:12] Rachel Kim: Are you seeing any correlation with specific models? Like the larger ones or function calling?

[10:18] Lena Hart: Mostly it’s our chat route. Model is “ri-large-chat” pinned. And yes, some tool calls.

[10:28] Sean Gallagher: Okay. The mitigation we did is independent of model, more gateway side. But we’ll check if one model cluster has higher resets.

[10:38] Priya Shah: One more: are you using streaming over websockets or SSE?

[10:42] Lena Hart: SSE.

[10:45] Priya Shah: Okay. Capturing.

[10:48] Nate Wong: If we disable HTTP/2, do we lose anything? Like performance?

[10:53] Sean Gallagher: Potentially a small efficiency loss, but for stability it’s worth it during an incident. It’s intended as temporary.

[11:04] Rachel Kim: And we’ll mark it as temporary in the doc.

[11:08] Priya Desai: What about switching regions? Can we route to us-west as a fallback?

[11:13] Sean Gallagher: You could, but that may add latency and also changes behavior. If you do, do it selectively (only for affected flows) and be aware of data residency or contract constraints.

[11:25] Rachel Kim: For Acme specifically, do you have constraints about staying in us-east?

[11:28] Miguel Santos: Not strict. We can failover for a subset of traffic.

[11:33] Rachel Kim: Okay. We can include that as a “if needed” option: route a portion to us-west if errors exceed threshold, but we’ll treat it as last resort.

[11:45] Owen Phillips: If you do cross-region, please note it in the ticket so we don’t misinterpret your metrics.

[11:52] Lena Hart: Makes sense.

[12:00] Sean Gallagher: Let me ask: are you using any custom keepalive settings? Like TCP keepalive or Envoy ping?

[12:06] Miguel Santos: We have keepalive but I’m not sure exact. We can check. Why?

[12:11] Sean Gallagher: Sometimes aggressive keepalive + intermediaries can cause resets. But again, I don’t want to send you on a wild goose chase. Disabling H2 is the simplest high-signal test.

[12:24] Rachel Kim: We’ll do one change at a time.

[12:27] (crosstalk)

[12:28] Priya Desai: Sorry—just to confirm, you’re saying this is on your side primarily, not ours.

[12:33] Sean Gallagher: We believe the primary trigger is on our side, yes. Your proxy setup can make it worse or more visible. But you are not the cause.

[12:44] Rachel Kim: And that’s what we’ll say in the email: “We’re seeing elevated streaming connection resets in us-east; Redwood is mitigating; in parallel we recommend a temporary client-side mitigation.”

[12:57] Lena Hart: Okay.

[13:00] Priya Shah: I’ll draft the workaround steps and send you for quick confirmation.

[13:05] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk next steps and ownership. Owen, can you ensure SUP-1842 has everything and is linked to any incident bridge internally?

[13:13] Owen Phillips: Yes. I’ll make sure the Slack bridge has the SUP pinned and the ticket has links back. I’ll also note the agreed comms cadence.

[13:22] Rachel Kim: Sean, can you commit to sending a short customer-safe root cause statement once you’re confident?

[13:28] Sean Gallagher: Yes. I can send a brief status within a few hours, and a better statement once we confirm.

[13:36] Miguel Santos: What’s the ETA to full resolution?

[13:40] Sean Gallagher: I can’t give an ETA. We’re actively reducing the resets, but until it’s stable for a sustained window, no ETA.

[13:49] Rachel Kim: We’ll avoid ETA promises. But we’ll keep cadence.

[13:54] Nate Wong: Can you also clarify whether retries could be causing any quota issues? We saw some 429s earlier.

[14:01] Owen Phillips: Retries can push you into rate limits. We can look at your headers and account limits. But for this call, we’re focused on streaming. Still, please note if 429s spike.

[14:13] Lena Hart: Okay.

[14:15] Rachel Kim: Let’s do a quick round: what do you need from us right after this call?

[14:21] Priya Desai: Email recap. Hourly updates. And that workaround doc.

[14:27] Miguel Santos: And a way to correlate your metrics with ours—request IDs.

[14:32] Rachel Kim: You’ll have those.

[14:34] Sean Gallagher: For request IDs, send in SUP-1842. Priya, can you include a snippet showing how to log headers?

[14:41] Priya Shah: Yup, I’ll include an Envoy example and a Node fetch example.

[14:47] Lena Hart: Great.

[14:49] Rachel Kim: We’ll schedule a follow-up tomorrow same time, 30 minutes, to review impact.

[14:56] Priya Desai: Works.

[15:00] (brief pause)

[15:02] Sean Gallagher: One more ask: if you can provide a couple of raw timestamps in UTC aligned with your logs, we can compare to our deploy and gateway events.

[15:11] Miguel Santos: Yes. We’ll send a small list.

[15:15] Rachel Kim: Perfect. Any other questions?

[15:18] Lena Hart: Just one—if we disable HTTP/2 and it doesn’t help, what’s next?

[15:23] Sean Gallagher: Next would be: (1) routing a subset to another region, (2) changing streaming chunk timeout behavior on your side, and (3) we may apply additional gateway config. We’ll decide based on metrics.

[15:37] Owen Phillips: And if error rate crosses a threshold or you have major business impact, we escalate to a Sev-level incident internally and consider status page.

[15:46] Rachel Kim: Alright. I’ll send the email recap right after. Priya will update the ticket. Miguel and Lena, please run the H1.1 change and report back in SUP-1842. Thanks all.

[15:58] Miguel Santos: Thanks.

[15:59] Lena Hart: Thanks everyone.

[16:00] (call continues with light scheduling chatter; recording ends)
